newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Brazil coffee harvest picks up but not quality.
newsitem.headline: Brazil coffee harvest picks up but not quality.

text.p: Harvesting conditions in most Brazilian coffee regions have improved over the past two weeks as rains have moved on but producers and traders said they still remain pessimistic about quality.
"The quality is terrible. It is very difficult to work with," said Oswaldo Aranha, president of the Brazilian Coffee Exporters' Federation who also has a farm in southern Minas Gerais state.
In the south of Minas Gerais, rains have held off for the past week and harvesting has resumed again, said an official at the cooperative in Varginha.
But of the coffee that has arrived at the cooperative, there has been a high proportion of green beans, he added.
In Sao Sebastiao do Paraiso, further north, there have been no rains for the past fortnight and the harvest is now settling into a more normal rhythm.
"But this has been a very abnormal year. By the end of June, I would say we had only 15 percent of the harvest in. Last year we had much more coffee," one agronomist said.
At present green beans account for 20 to 25 percent of coffee which is impacting on overall quality, he said.

In the Cerrado region, the harvest has picked up, with around 30 percent of the crop in by the end of last month, in line with previous years, according to an official at the Cerrado Growers' Association (Caccer).
But quality is disappointing and producers are reporting that quantity is also less than expected, she added.
In Marilia, southwest Sao Paulo state, rains have also held off in recent days but the soil is very damp which is delaying the drying process of beans knocked off by last month's heavy downpours.

"For the time being we haven't seen many rain-damaged beans as those beans which were hit by the rains haven't started to arrive yet as they are still drying out," said an agronomist at the local cooperative.
In Parana state, rains had returned this week, with only one day of sunshine, said Carlos Fadoni at the Maringa cooperative.
"The month of June has been horrible for us. There is very little coffee arriving as people are not being able to dry beans," he said.
Santos export firm Icatu/Sumatra estimated this week that around 40 percent of the total crop has been brought in, most of which was from Parana and Espirito Santo states.

"Quality-wise for Group I until the present time there is a high percentage of rain damage due to heavy precipitation causing beans to fall off the ground, plus hampering the drying process as well as harvesting," it said in a report.
The delays in harvesting have impacted on exports, with June shipments now expected to be under one million bags, despite sales registrations of over 1.34 million 60-kg bags to June 20.
"The low volume of June exports is a bit surprising since registrations and expectations were much higher but it confirms the delays in the incoming harvest," Icatu/Sumatra said.
